title: Wanting some advice on starting game dev with AI
author: PandoTheGamer
selftext:
So to start, I essentially have no experience in game dev. I want to make a pixel art JRPG kind of game and possibly in the HD-2D style. I want to use Unreal Engine, as I already have some familiarity with it.

About two years ago I tried getting into game dev, but thought I was never accomplishing anything through hours of YouTube tutorials, making me quit. But now I’ve been hearing a lot about AI use in game dev, and feel like it may make game dev feel a lot better to me.

So my question is essentially how should I use AI? As a teacher? As an artist? As a coder (which I’m not sure how you get that to work with Unreal)?

I’d love some advice and also just want to say that these advancements in AI are crazy.

comments.author: johnesco
comments.body: Don't pick an engine. Design the game in text in as much detail as you can before you actually start making mechanics or using assets. Be flexible at first unless there is a specific look you want. Design that look first. Then the engine you need will tumble out of it, and with AI there is a consider amount you do with no engine.

comments.author: CruelAngelsThesaurus
comments.body:
It'd help to know literally anything about game design first so you don't come back in here with slop that a 9 year old could make on Java in a night.

If you do that you're already setting the bar higher than 90% of the people here.

replies.author: PandoTheGamer
replies.body: I see what your saying, definitely something to keep in mind

comments.author: Embarrassed_Text_347
comments.body: My advice is to just start building, but not necessarily your dream game first. Build something simple to practice and hone in the skills required for your game. Don't try to make your dream game on your first attempt.

replies.author: PandoTheGamer
replies.body: I was kinda thinking that. Figured I make a very generic little game in normal 2D before doing something larger

replies.author: johnesco
replies.body: I agree, even if you never show it to anyone, just by trying to put it together you'll run into a lot of challenges. Solve those, learn, and the game you made doesn't matter, it's what you learned from it.

replies.author: deege
replies.body: This is good advice. Start simple with an old school game. The more you can do without AI the better, because it will give you a foundation for directing an AI later.

comments.author: Seven-Prime
comments.body:
Have AI build out the plan first. Help it figure out WHAT type of game you want. Then plan out how you'll break the game down into chunks. Then make it do the chunks. One at time.

You basically become a project manager or product owner.

comments.author: aftchans
comments.body:
I find claude voice is really good for picking up ideas quickly, great for planning you can ramble have you ideas consolidated and be picked apart in real time and at voice speed rather than typing. Helps keep you on track and work out what needs to be solved, then you can keep asking questions about whatever is technical or you don't understand yet and it explains pretty well. If you dont understand just clarify more. 

You can just info dump and explore here, flesh out everything you want, find gaps and flesh them out, then ask it to generate you a proposal based on everything you've fleshed out, then hand it over to a builder. 

But yeah as other have said you's need to run a bunch of session dedicated to lots of different tasks, planning, story writing, coding and art generation and then coordinating them all together.

comments.author: flavorgenerator
comments.body:
You can definitely do it with almost no skill. I made a whole tutorial on this, give it a try. No code skills required and I show everything you have to do

[https://youtu.be/3e-IynUFZuk?si=ArYLZazt7DH450eW](https://youtu.be/3e-IynUFZuk?si=ArYLZazt7DH450eW)

comments.author: 3tt07kjt
comments.body:
There are a lot of ways to use it. I would start with planning, coding, and code review. Start with existing asset packs (free ones). Use an engine (Unreal, Unity, Godot are all fine). 

Your process will change and adapt as you work on your project.

comments.author: wadrasil
comments.body: I used ai to compile a driver that works with allegro in freedos so I can use something that is not going to change next week but has the source code available. No idea if it's going to help. But using tools that are well documented help alot.

comments.author: Turbulent-Armadillo9
comments.body:
I never did game dev up until about a year ago.

I started just putting all my ideas into chat gpt. Asked a lot of questions, learned from YouTube. I started making a 2D platformer and it was really hard to know where to begin.

First I just drew a pixel art character on aseprite (pixel art) and a walk and jump animation. I made a platform he could walk and jump on and from there with the help ai and youtube everything has been unfolding pretty naturally. I was like okay now I need an enemy to kill so I animated a kick animation and made an enemy that walked and attacked…. Realized I needed hurt and death animations for enemy and player character… then I realized I needed a health system… the. Health pickups. 

Just like that things seemed to make sense. The hardest part was starting. 

If you aren’t getting good results from ai then IMHO you just aren’t doing enough manually and / or learning enough about how your game works because. People are one-shot promoting games which is cool but imho you really need to learn how to design and make a game, otherwise you won’t grow as a dev and it’ll probably just be slop.

Good luck. IMHO unreal seems a bit much for making something 2d but engines are just engines and learning it could be nice for future projects.

I’d suggest not making some pure ai code all in one file thing. Using an engine seems like a good idea to me.

replies.author: PandoTheGamer
replies.body: Another thing to keep in mind, thanks!

comments.author: Livid_Shallot5701
comments.body: Don't think ai is gonna think of everything. I'm fact YOU have to think of everything and tell it ai in a way it makes it right. So probably 2000 long and detailed prompts per small game

comments.author: mikenizo808
comments.body:
I agree with the others that you should refine your idea and perhaps make a browser game as a one-shot. Then you can play that anywhere and develop ideas. Be sure to ask for the source code too.

Then when ready, you can try your idea out in Unreal. You mentioned you already have experience with Unreal so that is great, but you really only need to install it and select an Unreal default template style. Then you can point your model to the `Unreal MCP`.

You will need Unreal 5.8 to use the Unreal MCP. Also, you should install Visual Studio Code 2026 as this has the required MSVC 14.50 (if I recall) you will need if your project starts adding C++ code, etc.

You should ideally have both the CLI and the App for your model. For example, both the Codex CLI and Codex App.  With the current models you can run Unreal completely with Control my computer features. However, it is best to start using just the Unreal terminal and prompting one prompt at a time.

To get motivation, see the Unreal conference video from this year which has a nice section on AI and the Unreal MCP. [https://www.unrealengine.com/news/state-of-unreal-2026-top-news-from-the-show](https://www.unrealengine.com/news/state-of-unreal-2026-top-news-from-the-show)

To learn how to start using it in a project, just search for Unreal MCP on youtube such as:

[https://youtu.be/f8qda6K089s?si=TMLx3NA4BOVDp23g](https://youtu.be/f8qda6K089s?si=TMLx3NA4BOVDp23g)

It is best to start with one of the default Unreal Templates that come with it. To choose what kind of map you want, consult the Unreal AI site, which is very useful and knows exactly what you are looking for.

[https://dev.epicgames.com/community/assistant/unreal-engine](https://dev.epicgames.com/community/assistant/unreal-engine)

Optionally, configure a local loreserver (similar to git, but is unreal-aware).
[https://epicgames.github.io/lore/tutorials/quickstart/](https://epicgames.github.io/lore/tutorials/quickstart/)

For artwork, start by letting your model create some cheesy 2d art. Then later you can install Blender (which is free) and let your model control that to create your art.

Finally, get a backup strategy such as a Lacie USB drive and also perhaps cloud. With all of these things in order there are no obstacles.

comments.author: deadcourtyard
comments.body:
Just get started.   
Speaking from experience, AI can come up with some really cool solutions, especially when you're learning to work with a specific technology or field. But paradoxically, it can easily lead you into a development dead end—issues might crop up that really should have been anticipated during the planning stage. In any case, you'll gain valuable experience—even if it means having to abandon a few projects along the way.

So just start, and everything will work out :)

comments.author: YannLeCoomer
comments.body:
I’m gonna give you some nontechnical advice. Nobody is gonna wanna see your ai generated concept art, nobody is gonna wanna read your ai-assisted script.

You need something extremely visually interesting that was clearly effortful and works  before they’re going to want to consume it at all.

Until you make something that generates  curiosity and, let’s be honest, a hit of dopamine on the viewers’ terms, asking someone to consider ai generated content is asking them a favor. Yes even your friends and family, yes even on this sub and in the discord.

replies.author: YannLeCoomer
replies.body: Also I’m not saying this to be mean I’m saying this so you don’t annoy your friends and get disappointed. Save the updates for the BIG stuff, like a fully playable demo, and they’ll listen.

comments.author: StarMonkeyGames
comments.body:
AI will code for you, it can tell you what game mechanics are. But it doesn't have good taste. 

The other thing is marketing. No one is going to see your game unless you go public with it. Even good games will be obscure. Start working on marketing early.

If you got a YouTube channel, lemme know. We can compare games and stuff
